Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Negative Appraisals.value: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down
I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I have permanently changed for the worse

vignette:
Eleanor Whitmore, a seventy-year-old widow and the manager of a mid-sized boutique hotel, had spent forty years building a reputation for grace under pressure. That composure shattered one evening eighteen months ago, when a misunderstanding over a guest complaint escalated into a confrontation with two police officers called to the property. She had tried to de-escalate, stepping between the officers and a frightened young front-desk clerk, and one of them shoved her hard against the wall, then dragged her by the arm out to the sidewalk while the other pinned her face-down on the asphalt. The arrest was quickly dropped—no charges were ever filed—but the memory had not dropped. It remained clear and detailed in every sensory dimension: the grit of the pavement against her cheek, the weight of a knee in her lower back, the officer’s clipped radio voice calling for backup, the faint smell of burnt coffee from a nearby patrol car. Remembering it brought back the same raw terror she had felt at the moment, a surge of helplessness that left her breathless and trembling as if it were happening again.

In the months that followed, Eleanor began noticing that something as ordinary as a crowded lobby could instantly drag her back into that scene without any warning. A cluster of guests checking in, a raised voice at the front desk, the sudden press of bodies near the elevator bank—each felt like a trigger, and before she could brace herself the memory would crash in, vivid and unbidden, flooding her with adrenaline and that crushing sense of powerlessness. She started delegating the busy check-in hours to her assistant, retreating to her office when the hotel became too full. But the triggers did not only come from crowds. The anniversary of the incident was approaching, and as the date drew nearer she found herself unable to shake intrusive thoughts about the officers’ faces, the crackle of their radios, the way one of them had smirked. These thoughts fed a growing conviction that the institutions meant to protect her—the police, the justice system, even the hotel chain that had offered no real support—had failed her completely. She began to mutter to herself, “No one was held accountable,” and each repetition of the thought sharpened the memory, made it more immediate, more damning.

And when she recalled the event, the terror was so acute that she felt as though she had permanently changed for the worse, that the confident, decisive woman who had once handled a fire drill and a disgruntled guest with equal calm was gone. She did not know herself anymore. This sense of identity loss made the memories heavier, more intrusive, because they now carried the weight of a life before that she could not get back. Eleanor would catch her reflection in the mirror and think, That is not me, which only made the next unwanted memory more vivid, more terrifying. The loops tightened: a trigger—say, a police cruiser idling outside the hotel—would remind her of institutional failure, which would bring the memory flooding back with full terror, which would then reinforce her belief that she was damaged beyond repair. Each episode deepened her conviction that she was permanently altered, and that conviction, in turn, made her hypervigilant for any sign of police presence or crowded space, feeding the cycle.

Her work suffered. She had always prided herself on walking the floor, greeting guests, smoothing over complaints, but now she avoided the public areas, and her staff noticed. One morning she found herself sobbing in the supply closet after a guest accidentally brushed against her in the hallway. That afternoon she called her primary care physician, who referred her to a trauma specialist. Eleanor arrived at the first session with a single question: she wanted to know if there was any chance she could feel like herself again, or if the woman she had been was gone for good. What frightened her most was the possibility that the permanent damage she feared was already a fact, and that the anniversary—now just two weeks away—would only prove it.
